Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

We introduce a family of rings of symmetric functions depending on an infinite sequence of parameters. A distinguished basis of such a ring is comprised by analogues of the Schur functions. The corresponding structure coefficients are polynomials in the parameters which we call the Littlewood-Richardson polynomials. We give a combinatorial rule for their calculation by modifying an earlier result of B. Sagan and the author. The new rule provides a formula for these polynomials which is manifestly positive in the sense of W. Graham. We apply this formula for the calculation of the product of equivariant Schubert classes on Grassmannians which implies a stability property of the structure coefficients. The first manifestly positive formula for such an expansion was given by A. Knutson and T. Tao by using combinatorics of puzzles while the stability property was not apparent from that formula. We also use the Littlewood-Richardson polynomials to describe the multiplication rule in the algebra of the Casimir elements for the general linear Lie algebra in the basis of the quantum immanants constructed by A. Okounkov and G. Olshanski.

The structure coefficients for multiplication in this basis are referred to as Littlewood–Richardson polynomials. These polynomials are computed through a modification of an earlier combinatorial rule, yielding an explicit formula that is manifestly positive in the sense of W. Graham.

The resulting formula has significant applications in both geometry and representation theory. In equivariant Schubert calculus, it describes products of equivariant Schubert classes on Grassmannians and reveals a stability property that is not evident from the earlier puzzle-based formula developed by A. We develop a parameter-dependent ring of symmetric functions, denoted \(\Lambda(x\|a)\), which extends the usual ring of symmetric functions. Its distinguished basis consists of double, or factorial, Schur functions \(s_\lambda(x\|a)\), indexed by partitions. These functions specialize to ordinary Schur functions when the parameter sequence \(a\) is set to zero. The multiplication constants in this basis,
\[
s_\lambda(x\|a)s_\mu(x\|a)
   =\sum_\nu c_{\lambda\mu}^{\nu}(a)\,s_\nu(x\|a),
\]
are polynomial deformations of the classical Littlewood–Richardson coefficients and are therefore called Littlewood–Richardson polynomials.

A modified Littlewood–Richardson rule gives a direct combinatorial formula for the polynomials \(c_{\lambda\mu}^{\nu}(a)\). The rule is expressed through suitably decorated, or barred, tableaux and reduces to the classical tableau rule after the parameters are specialized to zero. Each admissible tableau contributes a product of parameter differences, so the formula displays the relevant positivity directly. In particular, after identifying these differences with simple roots, the coefficients become polynomials with nonnegative integer coefficients, making Graham positivity manifest rather than merely implied by geometric arguments.

These universal polynomials also govern equivariant Schubert calculus on Grassmannians. Under the appropriate specialization of the parameters to torus weights, the double Schur functions represent equivariant Schubert classes, while the Littlewood–Richardson polynomials specialize to the corresponding equivariant Schubert structure coefficients. The symmetric-function construction shows that these coefficients stabilize as the dimensions of the ambient spaces increase, providing stable formulas independent of a particular finite Grassmannian once the indexing partitions fit inside the relevant rectangle.

Finally, the same framework applies to the center of the universal enveloping algebra of \(\mathfrak{gl}_n\). Through the Harish–Chandra correspondence, factorial or shifted Schur functions are identified with the eigenvalue polynomials of quantum immanants, a distinguished family of higher Casimir elements. Consequently, the Littlewood–Richardson polynomials furnish explicit multiplication formulas for these Casimir elements in the quantum-immanant basis, linking symmetric functions, equivariant Schubert calculus, and the representation theory of general linear Lie algebras.

## Schur and Littlewood: Foundations of Symmetric Function Theory

The names Issai Schur and Dudley Littlewood are closely associated with the theory of symmetric functions, an area of mathematics that connects algebra, combinatorics, and representation theory. Central to this subject are **Schur functions**, which were introduced by Schur in his study of representations of symmetric and general linear groups.

A Schur function is a symmetric polynomial indexed by a partition. It may be defined using determinants, semistandard Young tableaux, or representation-theoretic characters. These equivalent descriptions make Schur functions especially powerful: they form a basis for the ring of symmetric functions while also encoding important combinatorial and algebraic information.

Littlewood helped develop this theory and, together with Archibald Richardson, introduced the **Littlewood–Richardson rule**. This rule describes how to multiply two Schur functions:

\[
s_\lambda s_\mu=\sum_\nu c_{\lambda\mu}^{\nu}s_\nu,
\]

where the coefficients \(c_{\lambda\mu}^{\nu}\), known as Littlewood–Richardson coefficients, are nonnegative integers. Combinatorially, they count certain skew Young tableaux. In representation theory, they describe how tensor products of irreducible polynomial representations decompose into irreducible components.

For example,

\[
s_{(1)}s_{(1)}=s_{(2)}+s_{(1,1)}.
\]

This identity reflects the decomposition of the tensor square of the defining representation into its symmetric and exterior squares.

Littlewood also contributed to identities involving Schur functions, classical groups, and symmetric polynomials. His work helped reveal that these objects are not merely formal expressions: they provide a common language for studying tableaux, group representations, geometry, and algebraic structures.

Thus, the work of Schur and Littlewood lies at the heart of modern algebraic combinatorics. Schur functions supply the fundamental objects, while Littlewood’s contributions—particularly the Littlewood–Richardson rule—explain how those objects interact.

counterfactuals.output: We introduce a family of parameter-dependent symmetric functions that simultaneously generalizes classical Schur functions and several factorial or shifted analogues. Their multiplication is governed by Littlewood–Richardson polynomials—structure constants that depend polynomially on the deformation parameters and specialize to the classical Littlewood–Richardson coefficients. We establish combinatorial formulas, stability and vanishing properties, and a parameter-dependent Cauchy identity, yielding positivity in natural parameter differences. Geometrically, these functions represent equivariant Schubert classes, while the Littlewood–Richardson polynomials encode the corresponding equivariant intersection constants. We further connect suitable specializations with the eigenvalues and central characters of quantum immanants, providing a unified bridge between symmetric-function theory, equivariant Schubert calculus, and representation theory. This framework clarifies how deformation parameters record torus weights and offers effective tools for computing both equivariant Schubert products and spectral data associated with quantum immanants.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the main results of a mathematics article that gives a manifestly positive combinatorial rule for Littlewood–Richardson polynomials and proves stability of equivariant Schubert structure coefficients.
counterfactuals.output:
The article establishes two closely related results in equivariant Schubert calculus:

- **A positive rule for Littlewood–Richardson polynomials.** It expresses each polynomial as a sum over explicit combinatorial objects, with every object contributing a monomial—or a product of positive roots—with nonnegative coefficient. Thus positivity is visible term by term, rather than emerging only after cancellations. On forgetting the equivariant parameters, the formula reduces to the ordinary Littlewood–Richardson rule.

- **Stability of equivariant Schubert structure coefficients.** Under the natural embeddings obtained by enlarging the ambient flag variety, or equivalently by adding fixed points to the indexing permutations, the corresponding equivariant Schubert coefficients eventually stop changing, up to the expected relabeling of variables. The paper identifies these stable values with the Littlewood–Richardson polynomials governed by its combinatorial rule.

Together, the results show that a broad family of finite-rank equivariant Schubert multiplication constants is controlled by a single stable, manifestly positive combinatorial model. This both strengthens equivariant positivity and provides a practical way to compute the stabilized coefficients.

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe a new family of symmetric-function rings whose Schur-type basis has polynomial structure constants, including connections to Knutson–Tao puzzles and the Casimir algebra of \(\mathfrak{gl}_n\).
counterfactuals.output:
A useful family is formed by the **double, or factorial, symmetric-function rings**
\[
\Lambda(x\Vert a),
\]
where \(x=(x_1,x_2,\ldots)\) are the usual variables and \(a=(\ldots,a_{-1},a_0,a_1,\ldots)\) is a sequence of parameters. Their distinguished basis consists of **double Schur functions**
\[
s_\lambda(x\Vert a),
\]
defined by factorial alternants, tableaux, or divided-difference recursions. Setting all \(a_i=0\) recovers the ordinary ring \(\Lambda\) and the usual Schur functions.

Their multiplication has the form
\[
s_\lambda(x\Vert a)s_\mu(x\Vert a)
   =\sum_\nu c_{\lambda\mu}^{\nu}(a)\,
      s_\nu(x\Vert a),
\]
where the coefficients \(c_{\lambda\mu}^{\nu}(a)\) are **Littlewood–Richardson polynomials**. They specialize to the classical Littlewood–Richardson integers at \(a=0\), and, in geometric specializations, become equivariant Schubert structure constants. Although cancellations may appear in the \(a_i\), these coefficients are positive when written in suitable differences such as \(a_i-a_j\).

For partitions inside a rectangle, an appropriate quotient of \(\Lambda(x\Vert a)\) identifies with the torus-equivariant cohomology of a Grassmannian. Under this identification, the double Schur basis becomes the equivariant Schubert basis. Consequently, the coefficients can be computed by **equivariant Knutson–Tao puzzles**: triangular puzzles with boundary words determined by \(\lambda,\mu,\nu\), where ordinary pieces contribute \(1\) and equivariant pieces contribute parameter differences. Summing puzzle weights gives \(c_{\lambda\mu}^{\nu}(a)\).

There is also a shifted version of the theory. After the standard shift of variables and a specialization such as \(a_i\) linear in \(i\), double Schur functions become shifted or factorial Schur polynomials. Via the Harish–Chandra isomorphism, these correspond to central elements—higher Casimir operators or quantum immanants—in
\[
Z\!\left(U(\mathfrak{gl}_n)\right).
\]
Thus the same polynomial structure constants describe multiplication in a natural Schur-type basis of the Casimir algebra. The construction therefore unifies ordinary Littlewood–Richardson theory, equivariant Grassmannian calculus and puzzle rules, and the multiplication of higher Casimir elements for \(\mathfrak{gl}_n\).
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a journal-style abstract linking generalized Schur functions, Littlewood–Richardson polynomials, equivariant Grassmannian Schubert calculus, and Okounkov–Olshanski quantum immanants.
counterfactuals.output: We develop a unified framework connecting generalized Schur functions, Littlewood–Richardson polynomials, equivariant Schubert calculus on Grassmannians, and the quantum immanants of Okounkov–Olshanski. Using factorial (double) Schur functions as representatives of torus-equivariant Schubert classes, we identify the corresponding Littlewood–Richardson polynomials with the structure constants for multiplication in \(H_T^*(\mathrm{Gr}(k,n))\). Their stability, interpolation, and vanishing properties are then related to those of shifted Schur functions, which describe the central characters—and hence the eigenvalues—of quantum immanants in universal enveloping algebras. This comparison yields a common tableau-theoretic and specialization formalism: equivariant parameters encode geometric torus weights, while shifted spectral parameters encode highest-weight data. Within this formalism, positivity and triangularity in Grassmannian Schubert multiplication are placed alongside the Harish-Chandra images of quantum immanants, clarifying how both arise from the same generalized Schur calculus. The resulting dictionary links geometric intersection theory, polynomial Littlewood–Richardson rules, and noncommutative representation-theoretic central elements, and provides a natural mechanism for transporting identities among equivariant Schubert classes, factorial Schur functions, and quantum immanant eigenvalues.
